text:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used not only in teaching but also in educational administration. Schools and universities manage large amounts of information related to admissions, attendance, timetabling, finance, student support, and resource allocation. AI can improve the efficiency of these processes, although automated administration also raises concerns about transparency, fairness, and accountability.

One practical use of AI is the automation of routine enquiries. Chatbots can answer questions about deadlines, course registration, fees, and campus services. This may reduce administrative workload and provide students with support outside normal office hours. AI systems can also assist with scheduling classes, identifying timetable conflicts, and managing facilities.

Predictive analysis may help institutions identify students who are likely to withdraw or experience academic difficulty. By examining attendance, grades, and engagement patterns, administrators can direct support toward students who may need early intervention. When used carefully, this approach can improve retention and student welfare.

However, automated systems may produce unfair outcomes. An admissions or risk-assessment model may reflect historical patterns that disadvantage particular groups. If administrators cannot explain how a recommendation was produced, students may find it difficult to challenge the result.

There is also a danger of reducing students to data profiles. A person labelled as likely to fail may receive fewer opportunities or be treated with lower expectations. Predictions should therefore guide investigation rather than determine final decisions.

Educational institutions must define who is responsible when AI-supported decisions cause harm. Human review, clear appeal processes, and regular audits are necessary.

AI can make educational administration faster and more responsive. Nevertheless, efficiency should not replace fairness or accountability. Administrative AI should support human decision-makers while ensuring that students can understand, question, and appeal decisions that affect their education.
